concept.text: A proof or disproof that every nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function has real part 1/2. Sources given: https://www.claymath.org/millennium-problems/ ; https://world-of-mathematics.com/blog/millennium-problems-overview/.

page.title: Resolution of the Riemann hypothesis
page.definition: A proof or disproof settles whether every zero s of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s) in 0 < Re(s) < 1 has Re(s) = 1/2. Here ζ is the meromorphic continuation of ∑n≥1 n⁻ˢ from Re(s) > 1; zeros in that strip are called nontrivial.

goal.need: The primes thin out at a known average rate, but how far the count of primes up to x strays from that average is unproved. The hypothesis is equivalent to a deviation of order at most √x log x, close to the smallest possible; if it fails, the primes are far less regular than number theory assumes. Checking zeros by computer, or proving that a proportion lie on the line, leaves infinitely many undecided. Results such as a deterministic polynomial-time primality test need the wider hypothesis for other L-functions, which ζ alone does not give. No immediate practical application follows.

statements.quote: to emphasize the importance of working towards a solution of the deepest, most difficult problems
statements.context: One stated purpose of the Millennium Prize Problems, which include the Riemann hypothesis.

statements.body: Clay Mathematics Institute, official problem description by Enrico Bombieri
statements.quote: The failure of the Riemann hypothesis would create havoc in the distribution of prime numbers.

completion.title: Clay accepts a complete resolution of the Riemann hypothesis after its Millennium Prize examination.
completion.criterion: CMI determines under §7 of its prize rules that a complete solution answers its official problem, as Bombieri states it: the nontrivial zeros of ζ(s) have real part 1/2. ζ(s) is ∑n≥1 n⁻ˢ for Re(s) > 1, continued analytically to C; its trivial zeros are the negative even integers. A proof must cover every nontrivial zero; a counterexample must effectively resolve the problem under §5(c)(i). Consideration requires publication in a Qualifying Outlet, at least 2 years since publication and general acceptance; detailed review uses a committee of at least 3 members, including at least 2 experts. Extensions to other L-functions, including the generalized Riemann hypothesis, are outside this test.
completion.set_by: Clay Mathematics Institute, Bombieri’s official problem description and §§4–7 of the Millennium Prize Description and Rules adopted on 26 September 2018.
completion.threshold_quote: Second, a Proposed Solution must satisfy examination by CMI.
completion.basis: Bombieri’s description fixes the proposition; Clay’s rules make acceptance the institute’s own ruling after community acceptance, and address counterexamples. Clay’s Riemann hypothesis page still classifies the problem as unsolved. The announcement of 20 November 2026 is unsigned; it is hosted on the website of Levent Alpöge of Anthropic, whom Scientific American names as its author. It presents Lean files only; no written proof has been published in a refereed outlet. Scientific American reports that Andrew Sutherland of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology independently compiled the Lean files, and quotes him that the mathematical details of the proof remain to be understood. No CMI statement on the announcement had been reported as of 20 November 2026.

milestones.title: A proof establishes infinitely many zeta zeros with real part 1/2.
milestones.criterion: Prove that for every T > 0 there exists a real t > T with ζ(1/2 + it) = 0. Equivalently, the completed function Ξ(t), whose real zeros correspond to zeta zeros on Re(s) = 1/2, has infinitely many real zeros.
milestones.set_by: Analytic number theory’s convention of proved partial results; Hardy’s theorem, recalled and developed by Hardy and Littlewood in Acta Mathematica (1916), §1.4.
milestones.threshold_quote: has an infinity of real zeros.

milestones.title: A proof places more than five-twelfths of nontrivial zeta zeros on the critical line.
milestones.criterion: Prove κ = lim inf as T → ∞ of N₀(T)/N(T) > 5/12, where N counts nontrivial zeros with 0 < Im(s) ≤ T and N₀ counts those on Re(s) = 1/2, with multiplicity.
milestones.set_by: The field’s asymptotic zero-proportion benchmark, instantiated by Pratt, Robles, Zaharescu and Zeindler, Theorem 1.2.
milestones.threshold_quote: More than five-twelfths of the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta-function are on the critical line.

milestones.title: Rigorous computation verifies every zeta zero up to height 3,000,175,332,800 on the critical line.
milestones.criterion: Establish by rigorous computation that every nontrivial zero β + iγ with 0 < γ ≤ 3,000,175,332,800 has β = 1/2, including certification that no zeros were missed. Height is the dimensionless imaginary part γ.
milestones.set_by: The field’s finite-height verification convention, instantiated by Platt and Trudgian, Theorem 1.
milestones.threshold_quote: The Riemann hypothesis is true up to height 3 000 175 332 800.

milestones.title: A complete resolution survives two years of examination and gains general mathematical acceptance.
milestones.criterion: A complete proposed resolution gains general acceptance in the global mathematics community, as determined by CMI, after surviving rigorous community examination for at least two years. At least two years must also have elapsed since publication in a Qualifying Outlet. This is the first evaluation stage under §7(a)(i), preceding examination by CMI itself.
milestones.set_by: Clay Mathematics Institute, Millennium Prize Description and Rules, §§4(a–c) and 7(a)(i).
milestones.threshold_quote: general acceptance in the global mathematics community

milestones.title: A proof places a positive proportion of nontrivial zeta zeros on the critical line.
milestones.criterion: Prove κ = lim inf as T → ∞ of N₀(T)/N(T) > 0, where N(T) counts nontrivial zeros with 0 < Im(s) < T and N₀(T) counts those among them with Re(s) = 1/2.
milestones.set_by: Analytic number theory’s convention of proved partial results; Selberg’s 1942 theorem, as stated in the introduction of Pratt, Robles, Zaharescu and Zeindler.
milestones.threshold_quote: This means that a positive proportion of non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta-function lies on the critical line.

not_found: No prescribed sequence of intermediate zero-height or zero-proportion targets was found in Clay’s official problem description or prize rules.
Wiley redirected requests for the Platt–Trudgian full text to its abstract; the numerical theorem was available in the authors’ arXiv manuscript.
No statement by CMI on the announcement of 20 November 2026, and no publication of the claimed proof in a refereed outlet, was found as of that date.
Springer refused automated requests for the five-twelfths article; its text was read in the authors’ arXiv manuscript.

results.detail: The authors report a Lean 4 formalization, but its computational inputs use additional axioms asserting successful searches; Lean’s kernel does not check those runs. No peer review or independent replication is recorded.

results.finding: For all nontrivial zeta zeros asymptotically (no finite sample), the reported critical-line proportion is at least 0.67353820….
results.detail: The claimed proof includes a Lean 4 formalization, but successful computational searches are assumed through additional axioms rather than checked by Lean’s kernel. Confirmation remains false under the external-computation rule.

results.finding: For all nontrivial zeta zeros as T → ∞ (no finite sample), the reported simple critical-line proportion ≥ 0.67353820… exceeds five-twelfths.
results.detail: The authors report the theorem formalized in Lean 4, including analytic inputs, but rely on computational search assertions not checked by Lean’s kernel. This supports met with confirmed false under the stated rule.

results.finding: For zeta zeros over unbounded heights, the certified proportion bound κ ≥ 0.673639287955244058993397664145 entails infinitely many critical-line zeros.
results.detail: Infinitude follows mathematically from the reported positive proportion; the page does not state it as a separate theorem.

results.detail: Formal verification is reported through a kernel-verified Lean proof. The webpage is not a peer-reviewed paper.

results.detail: The source reports machine verification of all three required theorem statements; independent expert review is not recorded.

results.finding: For the asymptotic population of nontrivial zeta zeros, the certified κ ≥ 0.673639288166603967358714355985 exceeds five-twelfths.
results.detail: The source reports machine verification of all three required theorem statements; independent expert review is not recorded.

results.finding: For zeta zeros as T → ∞, the reported limiting lower proportion of simple critical-line zeros is ≥ 0.67385867.
results.detail: The imported results have AI review, with human verification outstanding. Numerical checks do not establish the analytic reductions or imported theorems; no proof-assistant verification or independent replication of the complete result is reported.

results.finding: For zeta zeros as T → ∞, the reported simple critical-line proportion ≥ 0.67385867 exceeds 5/12.
results.detail: The claimed proof relies on imported arithmetic, density, and stability results whose human verification remains outstanding. The supplied AI review and bounded numerical replication do not independently verify the complete zero-proportion theorem.

results.finding: For zeta zeros in asymptotically high intervals, the claimed positive proportion implies infinitely many critical-line zeros; no finite sample is used.
results.detail: The manuscript supplies an author proof. Its AI review and arithmetic checkers do not establish independent verification or a proof-assistant formalization.

results.finding: For asymptotic zeta-zero counts, the claimed short-interval theorem implies global κ ≥ 83/40800; no finite sample is used.
results.detail: The global bound is a consequence of summing the stated short-interval bounds. The analytic proof remains independently unverified; the supplied checkers verify only arithmetic and symbolic components.

results.finding: For asymptotic zeta-zero counts, the claimed proportion bound is 83/40800, below the required 5/12; no finite sample is used.
results.detail: Counting distinct odd zeros still gives a valid lower bound for the multiplicity-counted numerator, but the stated bound does not reach the required threshold.

results.finding: Across all sufficiently high intervals of length T^0.46680, simple critical-line zeros have a positive proportion, implying infinitely many such zeros.
results.detail: This is an asymptotic proof claim; no effective starting height is supplied. The posted acceptance report does not identify publication in a peer-reviewed journal.
results.quote: We prove lower bounds for simple critical zeros of the Riemann zeta function on all intervals of length (T^{0.46680}) and on almost all prescribed intervals whose expected zero count diverges.

results.finding: For all sufficiently high intervals of length T^0.475, the simple critical-line proportion exceeds 1.013%; tiling implies a positive global proportion.
results.detail: The numerical certificates were independently rerun, but those checks explicitly do not reproduce the asymptotic estimates. No peer-reviewed journal publication or proof-assistant verification is recorded.

results.finding: Across almost all prescribed windows with diverging expected zero count, distinct odd-order critical-line zeros exceed 8.63% of all zeros.
results.detail: The reported proportions fall below 5/12. Off-line density estimates also permit off-line zeros and do not supply the missing proportion bound.
